docs.heading: Q1: Why use an offline root CA?
docs.snippet: A: Limits blast radius -if an online issuing CA is compromised, you revoke the intermediate without trusting a potentially stolen root . Root signs intermediates rarely under dual-control ceremony .

docs.heading: 1. "Zero false positives is the goal."
docs.snippet: Wrong. Goal is actionable signal ; some FP cost is OK if triage is fast and gates are diff-based .

docs.topic: False Positive Management and Tool Rationalization
docs.heading: 2. "Developers should triage all SAST findings."
docs.snippet: Wrong. AppSec/champions tune rules; devs fix confirmed issues-don't dump raw scanner output.

docs.topic: False Positive Management and Tool Rationalization
docs.heading: 3. "Suppress = ignore forever."
docs.snippet: Wrong. Suppressions need expiry and re-review when code or rules change.

docs.topic: False Positive Management and Tool Rationalization
docs.heading: 4. "DAST finds everything SAST misses-skip SAST."
docs.snippet: Wrong. SAST catches secrets and dead paths early; DAST needs running app -complementary.
docs.text: 4. "dast finds everything sast misses-skip sast." wrong. sast catches secrets and dead paths early; dast needs running app -complementary.

docs.topic: False Positive Management and Tool Rationalization
docs.heading: 5. "High finding count proves program maturity."

docs.heading: L1 - Cluster trust model
docs.snippet: Attacker goals: steal secrets from etcd/API, escalate privileges via mis‑configured RBAC, escape to the node, move laterally through a flat network, or inject malicious code through untrusted images.
docs.text: l1 - cluster trust model attacker goals: steal secrets from etcd/api, escalate privileges via mis‑configured rbac, escape to the node, move laterally through a flat network, or inject malicious code through untrusted images. for a more intuitive understanding, refer back to the "kubernetes city" diagram above: the api server is the front desk, etcd is the city memory, and the scheduler/controller manager are the city planner and repair crew.

docs.heading: L2 - Image Security & Software Supply Chain
docs.snippet: Before a pod runs, you must ensure the container image itself is trustworthy. In the end‑to‑end workflow, this starts in the CI/CD Pipeline (image build & scan) and continues through the Image Registr
docs.text: l2 - image security & software supply chain before a pod runs, you must ensure the container image itself is trustworthy. in the end‑to‑end workflow, this starts in the ci/cd pipeline (image build & scan) and continues through the image registry and admission controllers .

docs.heading: 1. Build‑time scanning
docs.snippet: - Scan for CVEs with Trivy , Clair , or Snyk in the CI pipeline. - Break the build on critical/high vulnerabilities (set a severity threshold). - Generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for each
docs.text: 1. build‑time scanning - scan for cves with trivy , clair , or snyk in the ci pipeline. - break the build on critical/high vulnerabilities (set a severity threshold). - generate a software bill of materials (sbom) for each image (cyclonedx, spdx).

docs.heading: 2. Minimal base images
docs.snippet: - Use distroless , scratch , or Alpine images. - Remove shells, package managers, and unnecessary tools to reduce attack surface.
docs.text: 2. minimal base images - use distroless , scratch , or alpine images. - remove shells, package managers, and unnecessary tools to reduce attack surface.

docs.heading: 3. Cryptographic signing
docs.snippet: - Sign every image using Cosign (Sigstore). - Store signing keys in a KMS or use keyless signing with OIDC. - Verify signatures in the admission controller before the image runs.
docs.text: 3. cryptographic signing - sign every image using cosign (sigstore). - store signing keys in a kms or use keyless signing with oidc. - verify signatures in the admission controller before the image runs.

docs.heading: 4. Immutable image tags
docs.snippet: - Never use :latest in production. - Use digest references (image@sha256:...) for guaranteed immutability.
docs.text: 4. immutable image tags - never use :latest in production. - use digest references (image@sha256:...) for guaranteed immutability.

docs.heading: 5. Private registry
docs.snippet: - Store images in a private registry (Harbor, ECR, ACR, GCR). - Use imagePullSecrets scoped to specific namespaces. - Enable registry‑native vulnerability scanning as an extra layer.
docs.text: 5. private registry - store images in a private registry (harbor, ecr, acr, gcr). - use imagepullsecrets scoped to specific namespaces. - enable registry‑native vulnerability scanning as an extra layer.

docs.heading: 6. Admission policies
docs.snippet: - Reject images from untrusted registries. - Reject images with no digest or with mutable tags. - Reject images whose vulnerability scan results exceed the allowed threshold (via scanner integration).
docs.text: 6. admission policies - reject images from untrusted registries. - reject images with no digest or with mutable tags. - reject images whose vulnerability scan results exceed the allowed threshold (via scanner integration). interview gap: many candidates forget that image security begins in ci/cd, not after the pod is scheduled. the full chain - build, sign, scan, store, verify - is a must for senior roles. ---

docs.heading: L2 - Network policies, Ingress & Egress Security
docs.snippet: Network security must be enforced at multiple layers: intra‑cluster, ingress, and egress. Refer to the Network & Services block in the city diagram: the Service is the internal phone directory, the In
docs.text: l2 - network policies, ingress & egress security network security must be enforced at multiple layers: intra‑cluster, ingress, and egress. refer to the network & services block in the city diagram: the service is the internal phone directory, the ingress is the main gate. in the technical workflow, these sit after the pod is running, while network policies restrict pod‑to‑pod and pod‑to‑external traffic at the cni level.

docs.heading: 1. NetworkPolicy (Kubernetes native)
docs.snippet: - Default deny all ingress and egress , then explicitly allow what's needed. - Example: allow only DNS, API server, and specific services.
docs.text: 1. networkpolicy (kubernetes native) - default deny all ingress and egress , then explicitly allow what's needed. - example: allow only dns, api server, and specific services.

docs.heading: 2. Ingress Controller Security
docs.snippet: - Terminate TLS at the ingress point (use cert‑manager to automate certificates). - Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. - Configure WAF rules (e.g., ModSecurity with NGINX Ingress) or integrate a cloud WAF. - Res
docs.text: 2. ingress controller security - terminate tls at the ingress point (use cert‑manager to automate certificates). - redirect http to https. - configure waf rules (e.g., modsecurity with nginx ingress) or integrate a cloud waf. - restrict access by ip whitelisting, oauth2 proxy, or api keys.

docs.heading: 3. Egress Gateways
docs.snippet: - Control outbound traffic to external services using a dedicated egress proxy or firewall (e.g., Istio Egress Gateway, Calico egress policies). - Deny all egress by default and allow only approved en
docs.text: 3. egress gateways - control outbound traffic to external services using a dedicated egress proxy or firewall (e.g., istio egress gateway, calico egress policies). - deny all egress by default and allow only approved endpoints (api endpoints, monitoring systems, etc.).

docs.heading: 4. Service Mesh (Istio, Linkerd)
docs.snippet: - Enforce mTLS between all service‑to‑service communication automatically. - Implement fine‑grained L7 authorization policies (e.g., allow GET but not POST). - Enable observability and tracing with si
docs.text: 4. service mesh (istio, linkerd) - enforce mtls between all service‑to‑service communication automatically. - implement fine‑grained l7 authorization policies (e.g., allow get but not post). - enable observability and tracing with sidecars. interview gap: flat network inside a cluster is a common finding. an attacker who compromises one pod can reach any other pod. a staff‑level architect will describe a zero‑trust network with default‑deny and mtls

docs.heading: 1. Least privilege RBAC
docs.snippet: - Use Roles (namespaced) and ClusterRoles sparingly. - Never use cluster-admin for application workloads. - Implement break‑glass procedures with audit logging for emergency access.
docs.text: 1. least privilege rbac - use roles (namespaced) and clusterroles sparingly. - never use cluster-admin for application workloads. - implement break‑glass procedures with audit logging for emergency access.

docs.heading: 2. Service account token hardening
docs.snippet: - Disable auto‑mount of service account tokens unless the pod explicitly needs API access: - Use bound service account tokens (TokenRequest API) that are time‑limited and audience‑scoped, not the lega
docs.text: 2. service account token hardening - disable auto‑mount of service account tokens unless the pod explicitly needs api access: - use bound service account tokens (tokenrequest api) that are time‑limited and audience‑scoped, not the legacy long‑lived secrets. - employ projected volumes to combine multiple token sources with a single file.

docs.heading: 3. Enterprise identity integration
docs.snippet: - Integrate OIDC (Okta, Azure AD, Keycloak) for user authentication to the API server. - Use IRSA (AWS) or Workload Identity (GCP/Azure) to give pods a cloud IAM role without static credentials. - Thi
docs.text: 3. enterprise identity integration - integrate oidc (okta, azure ad, keycloak) for user authentication to the api server. - use irsa (aws) or workload identity (gcp/azure) to give pods a cloud iam role without static credentials. - this eliminates the need to store cloud keys in kubernetes secrets. attack scenario: a compromised pod with a mounted sa token can call the kubernetes api with that token's permissions. limit token permissions and disable a

docs.heading: L2 - Secrets Management & etcd
docs.text: l2 - secrets management & etcd

docs.heading: 1. Encryption at rest
docs.snippet: - Configure EncryptionConfiguration to encrypt secrets in etcd using a KMS plugin (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault). - Without this, secrets are stored as base64 (not encrypted) and can be r
docs.text: 1. encryption at rest - configure encryptionconfiguration to encrypt secrets in etcd using a kms plugin (aws kms, azure key vault, hashicorp vault). - without this, secrets are stored as base64 (not encrypted) and can be read by anyone with etcd access.

docs.heading: 2. External secrets
docs.snippet: - Never store secret YAML in Git . - Use External Secrets Operator or Sealed Secrets to sync secrets from a central vault into Kubernetes. - Alternatively, mount secrets directly into pods via CSI dri
docs.text: 2. external secrets - never store secret yaml in git . - use external secrets operator or sealed secrets to sync secrets from a central vault into kubernetes. - alternatively, mount secrets directly into pods via csi drivers (e.g., vault csi provider).

docs.heading: 3. etcd hardening
docs.snippet: - Restrict etcd network access (dedicated network, firewall rules). - Use mTLS for all communication with etcd. - Perform regular encrypted backups. - Enable audit logging on the API server to track w
docs.text: 3. etcd hardening - restrict etcd network access (dedicated network, firewall rules). - use mtls for all communication with etcd. - perform regular encrypted backups. - enable audit logging on the api server to track who accesses secrets. ---

docs.heading: L2 - Node & kubelet Hardening
docs.snippet: - Disable anonymous auth on kubelet (--anonymous-auth=false). - Disable the read‑only port (--read-only-port=0). - Enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin to limit kubelet's ability to modify its
docs.text: l2 - node & kubelet hardening - disable anonymous auth on kubelet (--anonymous-auth=false). - disable the read‑only port (--read-only-port=0). - enable the noderestriction admission plugin to limit kubelet's ability to modify its own node object. - use a minimal os (bottlerocket, cos, flatcar) with automated patching. - apply cis kubernetes benchmark settings using kube-bench.

docs.heading: Runtime detection on the node
docs.snippet: - Deploy Falco (eBPF‑based) to detect: - Unexpected shells in containers - Privilege escalation attempts - Unauthorized file access - Outbound connections to suspicious IPs - Forward Falco alerts to S
docs.text: runtime detection on the node - deploy falco (ebpf‑based) to detect: - unexpected shells in containers - privilege escalation attempts - unauthorized file access - outbound connections to suspicious ips - forward falco alerts to siem or notification channels. ---

docs.heading: L2 - Multi‑tenant Isolation
docs.snippet: - Namespace‑per‑tenant is the minimal baseline. - Use virtual clusters (vCluster) for stronger isolation (separate control plane per tenant). - Apply ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges to prevent noisy ne
docs.text: l2 - multi‑tenant isolation - namespace‑per‑tenant is the minimal baseline. - use virtual clusters (vcluster) for stronger isolation (separate control plane per tenant). - apply resourcequotas and limitranges to prevent noisy neighbours. - enforce networkpolicy per tenant namespace to isolate tenant workloads from each other. - use cilium with l7 policies if fine‑grained api‑level isolation is needed. - consider node pools or taint/tolerations

docs.heading: 60-second answer
docs.snippet: Q: How do you harden a Kubernetes cluster for production? A: Enforce Pod Security Admission (restricted) , admission policies (Kyverno/Gatekeeper) for image tags and securityContext, default-deny Netw
docs.text: 60-second answer q: how do you harden a kubernetes cluster for production? a: enforce pod security admission (restricted) , admission policies (kyverno/gatekeeper) for image tags and securitycontext, default-deny networkpolicies , least-privilege rbac , disable unneeded sa token mounts , encrypt etcd , run kube-bench , and runtime detection (falco). assume compromised pod -limit blast radius with network and iam boundaries. ---

docs.heading: Q1: PSA vs PSP?
docs.snippet: A: PodSecurityPolicy deprecated; Pod Security Admission uses namespace labels (enforce/audit/warn) with restricted/baseline/privileged levels.
docs.text: q1: psa vs psp? a: podsecuritypolicy deprecated; pod security admission uses namespace labels (enforce/audit/warn) with restricted/baseline/privileged levels.

docs.heading: Q2: OPA Gatekeeper vs Kyverno?
docs.snippet: A: Gatekeeper uses Rego ; Kyverno uses Kubernetes YAML policies-both validate/mutate at admission. Pick by team skill and policy complexity.
docs.text: q2: opa gatekeeper vs kyverno? a: gatekeeper uses rego ; kyverno uses kubernetes yaml policies-both validate/mutate at admission. pick by team skill and policy complexity.

docs.heading: Q3: Pod compromised-what limits damage?
docs.snippet: A: NetworkPolicy egress deny, non-root + read-only rootfs , minimal SA RBAC , no hostPath , metadata service not reachable from user-controlled fetchers, secrets not in env (prefer CSI with rotation).
docs.text: q3: pod compromised-what limits damage? a: networkpolicy egress deny, non-root + read-only rootfs , minimal sa rbac , no hostpath , metadata service not reachable from user-controlled fetchers, secrets not in env (prefer csi with rotation). ---

docs.heading: 2. "NetworkPolicy optional if we have a firewall."
docs.snippet: Wrong. East-west traffic inside cluster needs CNI policy -perimeter firewall doesn't see pod-to-pod.
docs.text: 2. "networkpolicy optional if we have a firewall." wrong. east-west traffic inside cluster needs cni policy -perimeter firewall doesn't see pod-to-pod.

docs.heading: 3. "Running as root in container is fine if cluster is private."
docs.snippet: Wrong. Container escape or supply-chain RCE → root on node amplifies impact.
docs.text: 3. "running as root in container is fine if cluster is private." wrong. container escape or supply-chain rce → root on node amplifies impact.

docs.text: 4. "service account tokens are harmless." wrong. default tokens may call kubernetes api -scope rbac and automount: false when unused.

docs.text: 5. "admission controllers slow clusters too much." wrong. policy at admit time prevents thousands of bad pods -optimize hot paths, cache policies.
